title: Tokenisation and vocabulary
goals: Encode and decode text under an explicit toy vocabulary
Explain how segmentation changes sequence length
Handle unsupported characters without silently deleting information

prerequisite.prompt: What information conditions a next-token distribution?
prerequisite.answer: The preceding token sequence, together with the model and any stated context. Changing segmentation changes that token sequence.

vocabulary: An item in a model vocabulary, which may represent a word, part of a word or another text unit
The permitted tokens and their identifiers
Mapping source text into a token sequence under a specified rule
Mapping a token sequence back to text under a specified rule

blocks.text: Tokens need not be words. A classroom tokenizer can use an exact, case-sensitive vocabulary and greedily choose the longest matching token from left to right. This is a toy rule, not a claim about every production tokenizer. Define IDs: 0=end, 1=cat, 2=c, 3=a, 4=t, 5=s, 6=space, 7=sat. The space token represents one literal space. The end token is a special terminator, not ordinary text.

At each position choose the longest matching ordinary token. If no token matches, stop and report the unsupported character and its position. Do not delete the character or guess a replacement. IDs identify entries; a larger ID does not mean a token is more valuable or more similar.

The encoding of cats sat is [1,5,6,7], followed by [0] only if the protocol appends an end token. Decoding concatenates the ordinary token strings to recover cats sat. Count four text tokens, or five sequence items with the end marker included; always state the counting convention. The two written words do not imply two tokens.

blocks.title: Keep the evidence roles separate
blocks.caption: Encoding preserves supported characters and makes unsupported input explicit.

lesson.title: Compare representations without changing the text

blocks.text: A character-only vocabulary c,a,t,s,space could encode cats sat as c,a,t,s,space,s,a,t: eight text tokens. The original vocabulary uses four. Both decode to the same source text. Sequence length is a property of the text, vocabulary and encoding rule together. Counts from different tokenizers are not automatically comparable.

In this vocabulary, sat is chosen over s because it is longer. The toy longest-match rule is defined explicitly. Real tokenizers may use different algorithms, byte encodings and special-token policies. Never infer an unknown tokenizer’s count from word count alone.

Supported case: cat encodes [1]; c at encodes [2,6,3,4]. A space changes both the character sequence and the possible matches. The input Cat is unsupported at position 0 because uppercase C has no entry. The input cat! encodes cat, then fails on ! at position 3; a partial encoding must not be reported as complete success.

blocks.label: Guided: encode c at, count its text tokens and explain how cat! should be reported.

blocks.text: Decoding round trips check representation, not factual meaning. A supported spelling can be false; an unsupported character can be important. Record the vocabulary version, rule and special-token convention when comparing counts or reproducing model inputs. Whitespace, case and punctuation are part of this exact toy input contract.

blocks.label: Exit: a program drops ! from cat! and announces a successful round trip. Identify the changed information and the honest response.

workbook.title: Read the contract
workbook.prompt: Explain why sat wins over s at the start of sat and why uppercase C is unsupported.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The rule chooses the longest matching ordinary token; sat has length three and s length one. Vocabulary and matching are case sensitive and contain no uppercase C.

workbook.title: Encode and decode
workbook.prompt: Encode cats sat using the given vocabulary, decode it, and count with and without an appended end marker.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Text IDs [1,5,6,7] decode cats sat. Four text tokens; five sequence items if the protocol appends end ID 0.

workbook.title: Compare sequence lengths
workbook.prompt: Encode cats sat with character tokens only. Explain the difference from four text tokens in the original vocabulary.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: c,a,t,s,space,s,a,t is eight text tokens. Larger chunks in the original vocabulary compress this representation; the source text is unchanged.

workbook.title: Trace a new input independently
workbook.prompt: Under the original vocabulary encode sat cats, decode it and count text tokens. Then trace sat cat! and state the exact failure position using zero-based character positions.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: sat cats encodes [7,6,1,5], decodes exactly and has four text tokens. sat cat! has partial IDs [7,6,1] then unsupported ! at position 7. Report failure with the partial trace, not complete success.

workbook.title: Audit silent repair
workbook.prompt: An encoder lowercases Cat and removes punctuation before encoding, but labels its output an exact encoding of the original. Explain what must be recorded or changed.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Lowercasing and punctuation removal alter the source. Record preprocessing separately and label the transformed text; an exact encoder under this contract must report unsupported characters rather than silently change them.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. All model outputs and probability tables are constructed classroom examples. No hosted AI service, external API or student account is needed. Distinguish a model objective from factual support and system permissions. Collect independent work before discussing its solutions.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Prepare the independent task and fresh retry without displaying solutions
sessions: Retrieve the prerequisite and distinguish a numerical claim from its interpretation.
Read section 1 and complete W1; ask for a reason alongside each answer.
Trace the worked case in section 2 and complete W2.
Discuss the diagram and complete W3 in pairs; record support.
Complete the guided response before sharing the answer.
Read the remaining sections and trace another constructed case.
Collect W4 independently, requiring calculations and a bounded conclusion.
Discuss W5 and the exit response. Provide feedback and a fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: c at gives [2,6,3,4], four text tokens. cat! fails on ! at zero-based position 3 after partial [1]. Exit: deleting ! changes the input; report unsupported punctuation or use a separately specified preprocessing/versioned vocabulary.
misconceptions: A token always equals a word
The vocabulary contains both whole strings and character pieces, so one word can take multiple tokens.
IDs are vocabulary indices; their numerical spacing does not establish meaning.
Dropping characters preserves an exact round trip
Deleted characters change the source and must not be hidden.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires [7,6,1,5], four text tokens and unsupported ! at position 7. Fresh retry: cats cat encodes [1,5,6,1], four text tokens; cats Cat fails at uppercase C position 5 after [1,5,6]. Require exact decoding and an explicit failure.
teacher.support: Provide labelled intermediate columns and allow a calculator. Ask students to state the meaning and denominator of a value before interpreting it. Extension: implement the classroom calculation locally and test boundary cases without using personal data.
teacher.next: Week 3 uses vocabulary alternatives to inspect next-token probability distributions and sequence probabilities.
